comparator.name: International Business
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–27 SBE EER Articles 12.1, 16.3 and 16.9 and Appendix IV control this general International Business example. Years 1 and 2 each contain eight 6.5 EC courses and two 4 EC skills units. Year 3 follows the published generic major pattern: 26 EC exchange, two 6.5 EC courses from one major, a 6.5 EC restricted elective, two 2 EC professional development units, 2.5 EC thesis preparation and an 8 EC individual thesis. The regulations publish major examples and identify separate Accounting and Entrepreneurship arrangements. The generic outline keeps the major and permitted electives as restricted choices. The current official course catalogue confirms the named units and their academic content. The EER takes precedence where public promotional material differs.
components: Quantitative Methods III (EBS2001, compulsory skills training)
Management of Operations and Product Development (EBC2022)
Choose a skills course from Maastricht’s approved fourth-semester list.
Study abroad semester at a partner university
The regular route requires 26 EC of approved study abroad. Students need at least 53.5 EC from Year 1 to apply and all 60 EC before departure.
First course in the chosen major

Choose two courses from one approved business major. Maastricht publishes options in accounting, finance, information management, supply chain management, marketing, organisation, strategy and entrepreneurship.
Second course in the chosen major
Take the second course from the same major. Maastricht specifies separate arrangements for some majors.
Choose one course from the approved quantitative economics, economics, ethics or law lists.
Writing a Bachelor's Thesis (EBS2080, thesis skills training)
The 2.5 EC skills course prepares students for the individual thesis.
The required thesis is an individual academic research paper worth 8 EC.

routeSelection.basis: The generic International Business target follows the published no-specialisation route. Emerging Markets has a separate enrolment choice and a different structure with an internship abroad. The EER publishes a common Year 3 template for the regular route, with major and elective courses chosen inside that structure. The common template is retained without selecting a particular major by UCR fit.

core: Management of organisations, marketing and strategy: Management of Organisations and Marketing, Strategy, Management of Organisations and Marketing Management, which teach how organisations are managed, how products are marketed and how business strategy is formed
Accounting and finance: Accounting and Financial Reporting, Finance and Managerial Finance and Accounting, covering financial reporting, corporate finance and financial decision-making

International business, economics and corporate governance: Economics and Business, Global Business and Corporate Governance, plus a compulsory study abroad semester, which place the firm in the international economy and in globalisation

Operations, supply chains, product development and information management: Fundamentals of Supply Chain Management, Management of Operations and Product Development and Management Information Systems, including the sourcing of raw materials and the management of business information
Entrepreneurship and small-business management: the compulsory Entrepreneurship and Small Business Management course and the Entrepreneurship major

Quantitative methods, philosophy of science and research training: Quantitative Methods I to III, Philosophy of Science and the thesis-writing skills training, which build the analytical and empirical skills of the programme

Business ethics, responsible management, law and corporate responsibility: the programme objectives on moral and ethical business behaviour and corporate social responsibility, and the programme description of law, taxation, ethics and globalisation as factors in running a business

Skills for working in international teams: teamwork, leadership, conflict resolution, presentation and intercultural communication, developed through the Management Game and the Professional Development skills trainings (Global Citizenship Skills and Leadership Skills)
Independent research and thesis: the 2.5-EC thesis-writing skills training and the 8-EC Bachelor's thesis in the final year
adjacent: Emerging Markets specialisation: a formal specialisation with an internship in an emerging economy, which connects economic development and business opportunities in emerging economies with their socio-economic, historical, cultural and political context and with responsible management and policy decisions

Formal third-year majors (Accounting, Finance, Information Management, Supply Chain Management, Marketing, Organisation, Strategy and Entrepreneurship), each of two courses, from which every regular International Business student chooses one
questions: How do international companies source raw materials, manage their people and finances, and make, market and sell their products across countries?
How do culture and politics shape the business environment and the responsible management of firms in rapidly developing countries?

trace: has teams develop a new venture from idea to final pitch through design thinking, market validation and business planning; it directly implements the entrepreneurship and small-business strand of the target (Entrepreneurship and Small Business Management) and its team-based learning by doing, and is the formal prerequisite of Strategy & Digital Transformation, International Business & Governance, Transnational Business Law, Money, Banking & Finance and Market Research

teaches research design, sampling and descriptive and inferential statistics including analysis of variance; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the quantitative-methods and research training of the target, whose own methods courses are not described on readable pages, and is the formal prerequisite of Marketing & Consumer Engagement, Public Economics, Econometrics, International Macroeconomics, Psychology of Organizations & Leadership, Negotiation & Strategic Thinking and Leadership & Diversity Management

introduces microeconomics (supply and demand, game theory, consumer behaviour, theory of the firm, market structure) and macroeconomics (output, unemployment, inflation); it directly implements the economic foundations that the target teaches in Economics and Business

teaches accounting theory and practice with emphasis on using and analysing financial statements and reading a corporate annual report; it directly implements the financial-reporting content of the target's Accounting and Financial Reporting

develops financial decision-making through case studies in which students analyse financial data, assess risk and take investment, budgeting and business decisions; it directly addresses the financial decision-making of the target's Finance and Managerial Finance and Accounting, without a full corporate-finance theory sequence

unpacks what drives consumer behaviour and engagement with brands, marketing strategy and brand strategy, including digital and AI-driven marketing, through cases and marketing plans; it directly implements the marketing strand of the target's Marketing Management and of Management of Organisations and Marketing, without a cross-country focus

has students develop a strategic plan from vision to execution using industry cases and examines the effect of digital technologies on strategy and business models; it directly implements the strategy strand of the target's Strategy

examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses, cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategy and global trade; it directly implements the international-business content of the target's Global Business and part of its Corporate Governance, and is the course of this programme most closely tied to the target's central subject

introduces the legal frameworks of cross-border trade, contracts, sales of goods and services, intellectual property, foreign investment and dispute resolution; it directly implements the business-law element that the programme names alongside taxation and ethics, without teaching tax law

explores the psychological, social and structural dynamics of organisations, including organisational behaviour, motivation, leadership, group dynamics and culture, with cases and skill-building; it directly implements the organisational-behaviour side of the target's Management of Organisations, without the management-theory and organisational-design content the target may teach

teaches negotiation through simulations and role-plays, including BATNA and interest-based negotiation; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the conflict-resolution and teamwork skills the programme develops, but it is a negotiation course rather than a conflict-resolution course

has students plan and carry out real market research, collect and analyse customer opinions and report results; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the marketing analysis of the target's Marketing Management and to its applied research skills, without covering international markets

studies national income, growth, inflation, unemployment, fiscal and monetary policy, business cycles, crises and international trade; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the international economic environment that the target addresses in Economics and Business and Global Business, at the level of national economies rather than firms

teaches the main ethical theories and practical ethics, including poverty and wealth, equality and climate change; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the moral and ethical business behaviour and corporate responsibility named in the target's programme objectives, although it is not a business-ethics course

introduces relational database management systems, SQL, normalisation and query processing; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the data-management part of the target's Management Information Systems, without information-systems strategy or business-process content

develops data cleaning, manipulation and visualisation and an own data-analysis research project; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the quantitative-analysis and business-information skills of the target's methods and information-management strands

teaches ordinary and generalised least squares and instrumental variables estimators, t, F and LM tests, Monte Carlo simulation in Stata and an empirical paper; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's quantitative-methods line and to its thesis preparation at greater econometric depth

analyses the effect of AI on competitiveness, innovation, labour markets and society and examines AI governance and ethics across marketing, human resources and finance; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the management of business information and responsible management in the target, without teaching information-systems management itself
Examines emotion regulation and psychological safety under pressure, including the role of cultural difference and inclusion in effective leadership.

evaluates the environmental, social and health impact of products, processes and services across their whole life cycle, from raw-material extraction to disposal or reuse, and develops strategic planning for circular systems; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's questions on sourcing raw materials and managing supply chains, without logistics or operations-management content

has student teams run a product-development project from customer needs to prototype, with defined team roles; it directly implements the product-development half of the target's Management of Operations and Product Development and its team-project skills, without operations management

teaches persuasion strategies, framing, nudging and the ethics of persuasion in business, media and politics; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the presentation and communication skills the programme develops, although it is not a business-communication course

introduces leadership fundamentals, including transformational and authentic leadership, with self-awareness and practical skills; it directly implements the leadership-skills development of the target's Professional Development: Leadership Skills

gives the tools to analyse and compare political systems and the effect of globalisation on democracies, using examples from around the world; it makes a specific complementary contribution to understanding how politics shapes the business environment in emerging economies, but it has no emerging-market or business content

teaches the schools of thought of International Relations and applies them to geopolitics, trade wars, south-south actors and global crises through a Security Council simulation; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the political context in which emerging economies integrate with the global economy, without economic content

examines the causes of violent conflict, including structural inequality, and theories of conflict transformation and peacebuilding; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the political fragility the specialisation associates with some emerging economies, without business content

gives the sociological concepts, methods and theories for analysing societies from the local scale to global interconnections, including their colonial and socio-historical context; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the social and cultural context of emerging economies, without economic content

examines how sociology developed within imperialism and colonial responses and the debates on modernity; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the historical and colonial context of development that the specialisation links to emerging economies, without economic content

covers social movement theories and environmental justice with case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas, including anti-colonial perspectives; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the social and environmental consequences of economic activity that responsible management in developing economies has to address

examines civil society, social capital and trust with cases from the Global South and Latin America; it makes a specific complementary contribution to how culture and society shape institutions in emerging economies, without economic content

studies the rise and fall of empires and great powers and the theories explaining them; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the historical background of global power relations that the specialisation connects with emerging economies, without economic-history content
Studies farming systems, agricultural innovation and trade-offs among production, biodiversity and resource use. This is a sector-specific application of sustainability in economic development.

examines how sustainability policies are made and enforced, which actors shape them and what makes policy effective; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the responsible management and policy decisions the specialisation prepares for, without a development focus

surveys legal systems and the main fields of law and is the formal prerequisite of Introduction to Public International Law; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the legal grounding for the international legal context of emerging economies, without business-law content

introduces public international law, including sources, self-determination, Third World Approaches to International Law and treaty negotiation; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the international legal order within which emerging economies operate, without business-law content

examines market failure, public goods, taxation, public spending, redistribution and political economy with empirical evidence on efficiency and equity; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the economic-development and policy questions of the specialisation, without development economics

alternatives.label: International Business, Strategy and Entrepreneurship
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has four business-function courses in marketing, strategy and the management of organisations (Marketing & Consumer Engagement, Strategy & Digital Transformation, Psychology of Organizations & Leadership, Market Research), two accounting and finance courses, four economics and international-business courses (Introduction to Economics, International Macroeconomics, International Business & Governance, Transnational Business Law), four leadership, negotiation and communication courses, Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations and Consumer Product Design, three research-methods, econometrics and data courses plus Database Management Systems, and further courses on AI and business, ethics and circular economy together with Personal & Professional Development. The label names the business, economics, leadership and entrepreneurship core with the business-law and data strands without presenting any one strand as the whole programme.
alternatives.concept: Study how firms operate across borders through accounting, finance, marketing, strategy, entrepreneurship and business law. Use data and research methods to examine customers, markets and business decisions.
progression: Six terms of four courses include Personal & Professional Development in Year 1 and 8 level-300 courses. The current workbook confirms offerings and earlier prerequisites.

alternatives.label: Business in Emerging Economies
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has seven business and economics courses (Introduction to Economics, International Macroeconomics, Public Economics, Econometrics, Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations, International Business & Governance, Transnational Business Law), three politics and international-relations courses, five sociology and history courses on colonial and Global South contexts, two law courses (Law, Society & Justice and Public International Law), three sustainability courses on governance, food supply chains and circular economy, Ethics, Leadership & Diversity Management, Research Methods & Statistics and Personal & Professional Development. The label therefore names the business and economics core together with the political, social, legal and sustainability context instead of presenting emerging markets or business alone as the whole programme, and the label's emerging-economies framing refers to the perspective of the courses, not to a dedicated development-economics curriculum.
alternatives.concept: Study how institutions, economic policy and social change shape business in emerging economies. Combine international business and economics with politics, law and sustainability, including applications to agriculture and environmental governance.
alternatives.distinctness: Alternative 1 organises the programme around the functions of an international firm (marketing, strategy, accounting and finance, leadership, operations and product development, information and entrepreneurship). Alternative 2 changes the organising question to how politics, culture, history and law shape business and economic development in emerging economies, which is the evidenced direction of the target's formal Emerging Markets specialisation. That change has material curricular consequences: marketing, strategy, accounting, finance, negotiation, product design, market research, database and data-science courses are replaced by comparative politics, international relations, peace and conflict, three sociology courses, history of empires, public international law, Public Economics and two sustainability courses on food supply chains and governance. The programmes share 11 courses and differ by 13 courses each, so every pair passes the 30 EC / 4-course floor in both directions.
traceOverrides: has teams develop a new venture from idea to final pitch with market validation and business planning, including business and social entrepreneurship; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the business-opportunity side of the specialisation, without any emerging-market content, and is the formal prerequisite of International Business & Governance and Transnational Business Law

introduces micro- and macroeconomics, the economic foundation of the specialisation's study of economic development and business opportunities; it makes a specific complementary contribution, without any development content

studies growth, inflation, unemployment, fiscal and monetary policy, business cycles, crises and international trade; it directly implements the macroeconomic and international-trade analysis the specialisation needs for economic development in emerging economies, without a development focus

examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses, cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategy and global trade; it directly implements the specialisation's question of how culture and politics shape business, but not its emerging-market focus

introduces the legal frameworks of cross-border trade, contracts, intellectual property, foreign investment and dispute resolution; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the legal environment of business in emerging economies, without addressing any particular legal system

teaches ordinary and generalised least squares and instrumental variables estimators and tests with an empirical paper in Stata; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the analytical skills the specialisation uses to understand economic development, without development data

teaches the main ethical theories and practical ethics, including poverty and wealth, equality and historical injustice; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the specialisation's responsible management and policy decisions in developing economies, although it is not a business-ethics course

explores how diverse perspectives and experiences shape effective leadership, with case studies and workshops; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the culture-sensitive management and cross-cultural collaboration the specialisation studies, without emerging-market content

evaluates the impact of products and processes across the life cycle from raw-material extraction to reuse; it makes a specific complementary contribution to responsible management of resources and supply chains in developing economies, without any regional focus

Organisation, leadership and cross-cultural communication (Organisation major)
Supply chain management and operations (Supply Chain Management major)

selection.assessment: Two UCR alternatives are defensible and production stopped at two. Alternative 1 owns thirteen generator-eligible rows that describe the target's own core (6035 to 6045 on international business and global markets, how international companies are managed, strategy, marketing, accounting and financial decision-making, supply chains and sourcing, managing employees, business law and taxation, business ethics, globalisation and business information management; 6047 on leadership in international organisations; 6048 on cross-cultural business communication). Alternative 2 is built on the five stable study directions in emerging markets (6050 to 6054), which are the target's formal Emerging Markets specialisation and form one coherent direction on economic development and the political and cultural context of business; it shares 11 courses with Alternative 1 and differs by 13 courses each way, so it passes the 30 EC / 4-course floor. A third concept was assessed on the formal Organisation major (people, leadership, negotiation and cross-cultural communication), supported by rows 6041, 6047, 6048 and 6049. Its evidence is already substantively covered by Alternative 1, which contains Psychology of Organizations & Leadership, Personal Leadership, Leadership & Diversity Management, Negotiation & Strategic Thinking and Persuasive Communication; a separate programme would keep those courses and replace the business-function courses with general psychology, rhetoric and behavioural-economics courses that the evidence does not tie to the target, so it was rejected as not-substantively-distinct. The Supply Chain Management major (row 6040) was rejected as not-feasible: UCR has no supply-chain, logistics or operations-management course (only Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy and Consumer Product Design touch the area, both already in Alternative 1), so the differing courses would be an assortment. The remaining majors (Accounting, Finance, Information Management, Marketing, Strategy and Entrepreneurship) are covered by the business-function courses of Alternative 1 and describe no different organising logic.

blocks: Management, organisations, marketing, strategy and leadership

Both address how organisations function and are managed; Psychology of Organizations & Leadership approaches this through organisational behaviour, motivation, group dynamics, culture and leadership, rather than through management theory or organisational design.

Both address marketing management; Marketing & Consumer Engagement covers consumer behaviour, marketing strategy, digital marketing and brand strategy with marketing plans, without a cross-country focus.
Both address business strategy; Strategy & Digital Transformation has students develop a strategic plan from vision to execution, with a digital-technology emphasis.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Management of Organisations and Marketing introduces organisations and marketing together; the UCR courses on each half are aligned with the larger Management of Organisations and Marketing Management components, and no further UCR course is a sufficiently direct counterpart.

Both develop leadership skills; Personal Leadership introduces transformational and authentic leadership with self-awareness and practical skills, which is the specific function of the Professional Development: Leadership Skills training, although it is a full course rather than a short training.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Management Game is a team-based management simulation skills training, and no scheduled UCR course is a sufficiently direct counterpart; Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations is a venture-creation course aligned with Entrepreneurship and Small Business Management.
Both teach financial reporting; Accounting & Corporate Finance covers accounting theory and practice with emphasis on using and analysing financial statements and annual reports.
Both study financial markets, asset pricing, and risk and return. Maastricht also develops the corporate investment perspective.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Managerial Finance and Accounting is a second-year course on management accounting and corporate finance; UCR's accounting and finance courses are already aligned with Accounting and Financial Reporting and Finance, and no other UCR course addresses managerial accounting.

Both give the economic foundations for business; Introduction to Economics covers micro- and macroeconomics, which is the economics part of Economics and Business, without the business-context applications.
International business, governance, law, ethics and responsible management

Both address international business; International Business & Governance examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses, global trade and cross-border governance, which is the central subject of Global Business.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Corporate Governance is a dedicated second-year course on the governance of firms; International Business & Governance covers cross-border governance but is already aligned with Global Business, and no other scheduled UCR course addresses corporate governance.
Operations, product development, information and data
UCR takes a consumer product from needs to prototype and considers production scaling. Maastricht also develops quantitative methods for operations and supply decisions.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Fundamentals of Supply Chain Management has no UCR counterpart; Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy addresses the life cycle of products from raw materials to reuse but not logistics, sourcing or supply-chain management.
UCR develops database design, SQL and data management skills. Maastricht studies how organisations use information systems for business processes and strategy.

Both address starting and running a small venture; Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations has teams develop a venture from idea to final pitch with market validation and business planning, without the small-business management content of the component.
Both use statistical inference and regression to analyse data. Maastricht’s skills course applies these methods to business case studies.
Politics, society, history and sustainability in emerging-economy contexts
Personal development, study abroad, majors and electives

notes.text: UCR offers courses in strategy, marketing, accounting, finance and entrepreneurship. Maastricht also requires dedicated work in supply chains, operations, management information systems and corporate governance, along with study abroad and an individual thesis.

The emerging economies option connects business with economic development, political institutions and sustainability. Maastricht’s formal Emerging Markets specialisation has a separate curriculum and an internship abroad.

audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht’s International Business bachelor examines how firms operate across borders through management, marketing, finance, strategy and operations. This example follows the regular route.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The first UCR option combines business functions with leadership, entrepreneurship and data. The second examines how institutions and economic development shape business in emerging economies. Maastricht’s regular route includes a major, a study abroad semester and an individual thesis.
